title: The Digestive System: From Bite to Energy
summary: How the body turns a bite of food into energy, step by step from the mouth to the stomach to the intestines.
poll: Chewing your food well is one of the most important parts of digestion.

versions.title: The Digestive System: From Bite to Energy
versions.text:
Do you like to eat snacks? Lots of kids do. But food must go on a long trip.

First, you chew your food. Your teeth cut it small. Then you swallow it. It goes down a long tube.

Next, the food goes to your stomach. Your stomach squeezes it hard. It mixes in juice. Soon the food turns to mush.

Then the mush moves on. It goes into long tubes. These are called intestines. Here your body takes out the good parts. These good parts give you energy.

The parts you do not need turn to waste. The waste leaves your body later.

This whole trip can take a day. Your body digests food every single day.

Chew your food well. It helps your body digest it!

versions.title: The Digestive System: From Bite to Energy
versions.text:
Do you know what happens to your food after you eat it? It goes on a long trip inside your body. The trip is called digestion.

First, you chew your food with your teeth. Chewing breaks the food into small bits. Soon you swallow it. It slides down a long tube.

Next, the food lands in your stomach. Your stomach squeezes the food. It mixes with juice inside. Soon the food turns into soft mush.

Then the mush moves into long tubes. These tubes are called intestines. Here your body takes out the good parts. These parts give you energy.

The parts your body does not need become waste. The waste leaves your body later.

This whole trip can take about a day. Your body digests food every day. That is how you get energy to play!

Have you ever thought about where your food goes after you swallow it? It goes on a long trip through your body. This trip is called digestion.

Digestion starts in your mouth. Chewing breaks big pieces of food into many small bits. This makes it much easier to swallow. The food then slides down a long tube. It lands in your stomach.

Inside your stomach, strong muscles squeeze the food. They turn it again and again, almost like a washing machine. Your stomach also mixes in strong juice. After a while, the food turns into a soft, thick mush.

That mush moves into long, winding tubes called intestines. These tubes are packed tightly inside your belly. Here your body pulls out the good parts of the food. These good parts are called nutrients. They give you energy to run, play, and grow.

Whatever your body cannot use turns into waste. This waste slowly leaves your body later on.

This whole trip can take about a day, from the first bite to the very end. Your body digests food every day. That gives you the energy you need to stay strong and healthy.

versions.title: The Digestive System: From Bite to Energy
versions.text:
Have you ever thought about where your food goes after you swallow it? That bite begins a long journey through your body called digestion. Digestion breaks food down into fuel your body can use.

Digestion starts in your mouth. Chewing breaks large pieces of food into many small bits, which is much easier for your body to handle. Your mouth also makes a juice called saliva. Saliva helps soften the food and makes it easier to swallow.

Once you swallow, the food slides down a long tube called the esophagus and arrives in your stomach. Your stomach squeezes and turns the food again and again, almost like a washing machine. It also mixes in strong digestive juices that break the food apart. Soon the food turns into a soft, wet mush.

Next, the mush travels into long, winding tubes called the intestines. Inside the small intestine, tiny helpers called enzymes break the food down even more. Your body then absorbs the good parts of the food, called nutrients, pulling them into your blood. These nutrients then travel all through your body, giving you energy to run, play, and grow.

Whatever your body cannot use becomes waste. This waste moves slowly through the large intestine and leaves your body.

The whole journey can take about a day, from the first bite to the very end. Your body digests food every day, turning meals into the energy you need to stay strong and healthy.

versions.title: The Digestive System: Turning Meals into Energy
versions.text:
Have you ever wondered what happens to a bite of food after you swallow it? That bite begins a remarkable journey through your body called digestion, the process that breaks food down into fuel your body can use for energy, growth, and repair.

Digestion begins the moment food enters your mouth. Chewing breaks large pieces of food into many small bits, which is far easier for the rest of your digestive system to manage efficiently. Glands inside your mouth also secrete a fluid called saliva, which begins breaking the food down chemically and makes it easier and safer to swallow.

Once you swallow, the food slides down a long, muscular tube called the esophagus and arrives in your stomach. Along the way, a wave-like squeezing motion called peristalsis pushes the food steadily forward. Your stomach churns the food again and again, almost like a washing machine, while secreting powerful acidic juices that break the food apart further. Within a few hours, the food has turned into a soft, thick mush known as chyme.

Next, that mush travels into long, winding tubes called the intestines. The inner wall of the small intestine is covered with tiny, finger-like structures called villi, which increase the surface area available for absorbing nutrients into the bloodstream. These nutrients then circulate throughout your body, supplying the energy your cells need to function and grow.

Whatever your body cannot use becomes waste material, which passes into the large intestine, sometimes called the colon. Here, extra water is reabsorbed before the remaining waste finally leaves your body.

The entire journey can take about a day, sometimes longer, from the first bite to the very end. Your body digests food every day, quietly turning your meals into the energy that keeps you strong, healthy, and ready to learn.

checklist: I explained the path food takes from the mouth to the small intestine.
I used the words esophagus and nutrient correctly.
I used at least two key words from the lesson in complete sentences.
MID.modelAnswer: After you chew and swallow food, it slides down a long tube called the esophagus and lands in your stomach, where it is squeezed and mixed with digestive juices until it becomes soft mush. That mush then moves into the small intestine, where the body absorbs the useful nutrients from the food and sends them into the bloodstream to give you energy.

keyWords.definition: the wave-like squeezing motion that pushes food through the digestive tract
keyWords.example: Peristalsis continues to move food forward even when you are lying down.

keyWords.definition: tiny, finger-like structures lining the small intestine that help absorb nutrients
keyWords.example: Villi increase the surface area of the intestine so more nutrients can be absorbed.

keyWords.definition: to release a liquid substance, such as a juice or fluid, from a gland or cell
keyWords.example: Sweat glands secrete fluid onto the skin to help cool the body.

keyWords.definition: another name for the large intestine, the last major part of the digestive tract
keyWords.example: Water is reabsorbed from waste material as it moves through the colon.

keyWords.definition: a body part that makes and releases a substance the body uses, such as saliva or acid
keyWords.example: A gland in the mouth produces saliva whenever you smell delicious food.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: The stomach is the single most essential organ in the entire body.
Digestion is a coordinated system that turns food into usable nutrients and energy.
Villi exist only to make the small intestine look different from the large intestine.
Peristalsis only occurs inside the esophagus.
questions.why: The article connects the mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, and large intestine into a coordinated system that converts food into nutrients and energy.

wrong.A: The stomach is one important step, but the article presents the whole system, not a single most essential organ.
wrong.C: Villi serve a functional purpose, absorbing nutrients, not merely a visual one.
wrong.D: The article states that peristalsis occurs throughout much of the digestive tract, not only in the esophagus.

questions.stem: According to the article, what is the main function of villi?
options: They increase the surface area available for absorbing nutrients.
They secrete acidic juices that break food apart in the stomach.
They push food forward through wave-like contractions of the gut.
They store waste material before it leaves the body.
questions.why: The article explains that villi, tiny finger-like structures, dramatically increase the surface area available for absorbing nutrients into the bloodstream.

wrong.B: Acidic juices are secreted in the stomach, not by villi.
wrong.C: Pushing food forward describes peristalsis, not villi.
wrong.D: Waste storage occurs later, in the large intestine.

questions.stem: What does the article say happens to waste material once it reaches the colon?
options: It is absorbed directly into the bloodstream, like a nutrient.
It is broken down further by tiny, finger-like villi.
Extra water is pulled back into the body.
It travels back up to the stomach through the esophagus.
questions.why: The article states that in the large intestine, also called the colon, extra water is reabsorbed back into the body before the remaining waste exits.

wrong.A: Nutrient absorption into the blood mainly happens earlier, in the small intestine.
wrong.B: Villi line the small intestine, not the colon.
wrong.D: Waste moves forward and out of the body, never back toward the stomach.

questions.stem: The article says glands in the mouth secrete saliva. What does secrete mean here?
options: To hide something carefully and completely out of sight
To chew food into very small bits with the teeth
To absorb a nutrient directly into the blood
To release a substance from a gland or cell
questions.why: The article uses secrete to describe glands releasing saliva, and similarly the stomach secreting acidic juices.

wrong.A: Secrete is about releasing, not concealing.
wrong.B: Chewing is a mechanical action done by the teeth.
wrong.C: Absorption happens later, in the small intestine, and is a different process.

questions.stem: What causes food to keep moving forward through the digestive tract, even when a person is lying down?
options: A wave-like muscle action called peristalsis.
Gravity alone pulls the food steadily downward.
Villi pull the food forward with tiny movements.
Saliva continues pushing the food from behind.
questions.why: The article explains that peristalsis, a wave-like squeezing motion, propels food forward regardless of the body's orientation.

wrong.B: The article specifically notes that food moves forward regardless of body orientation, which rules out gravity as the main cause.
wrong.C: Villi are involved in absorption, not in moving food forward.
wrong.D: Saliva acts only in the mouth, far earlier in the process.

questions.stem: Why does the small intestine need villi if food has already been broken down into chyme by the stomach?
options: Villi further digest food by chewing it into smaller pieces inside the gut.
Villi give the small intestine enough surface area to absorb nutrients.
Villi secrete the acid that originally broke down the food in the stomach.
Villi compact the leftover waste before it leaves the body each day.
questions.why: Even after food becomes chyme, nutrients still must be absorbed into the bloodstream, and villi provide the surface area needed for that absorption to happen efficiently.

wrong.A: Villi are not involved in chewing; that happens only in the mouth.
wrong.C: Acid secretion happens in the stomach, not from villi.
wrong.D: Waste compacting happens later, in the colon.

questions.stem: How is the role of the esophagus different from the role of the small intestine, according to the article?
options: The esophagus absorbs nutrients, while the small intestine only transports food.
The esophagus secretes digestive acid, while the small intestine stores waste.
The esophagus mainly transports food, while the small intestine mainly absorbs nutrients.
Both organs perform exactly the same function at different times.
questions.why: The article describes the esophagus as a tube that carries food down to the stomach, while the small intestine is where nutrients are absorbed into the bloodstream through the villi-lined walls.

wrong.A: This reverses the organs' actual roles described in the article.
wrong.B: Acid is secreted in the stomach, and waste is stored in the colon, not the small intestine.
wrong.D: The article clearly assigns different functions to each organ.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe digestion as a 'remarkable journey' rather than simply listing body parts?
options: To entertain readers with a fictional adventure story
To suggest that digestion is dangerous and should be avoided
To argue that one organ works completely alone, without the others
To help readers see digestion as one connected process
questions.why: Framing digestion as a journey helps readers follow food step by step through connected organs, understanding digestion as one continuous process.

wrong.A: The article describes real biology, not a fictional adventure.
wrong.B: The article presents digestion as a normal, healthy body process, not something dangerous.
wrong.C: The article shows multiple organs working together, not one organ acting alone.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how peristalsis and villi each play a different, important role in digestion. Use evidence from the article to support your explanation.
checklist: I explained the role of peristalsis in digestion.
I explained the role of villi in digestion.
I used precise vocabulary from the article and organized my answer in clear paragraphs.
HIGH.modelAnswer:
Peristalsis and villi both play essential but very different roles in digestion. Peristalsis is the wave-like squeezing motion that pushes food through the esophagus, stomach, and intestines, ensuring that food keeps moving forward through the digestive tract no matter how the body is positioned. Without peristalsis, food would not travel from one organ to the next.

Villi, on the other hand, do not move food forward; instead, they help the body absorb nutrients once food has already been broken down into chyme. These tiny, finger-like structures line the small intestine and dramatically increase its surface area, allowing far more nutrients to pass into the bloodstream than would be possible with a smooth intestinal wall. Together, peristalsis and villi show how digestion depends on both movement and absorption working in coordination.
